title: CSS 311: End-Semester Theory Mock Paper (Parts C, D, E)
instructions: Answer all three sections: Section 1 (Interconnection Networks), Section 2 (Vector Processors), and Section 3 (Performance Tools).
Show all intermediate derivations, formulas, and metric calculations.
Marks for each question and sub-question are indicated on the right.

sections.title: Section 1: Interconnection Networks (Part C)
sections.description: Graph-theoretic measures, topology metrics, E-cube routing, and graph embedding.

questions.question: An interconnection network is structured as a 4-ary 3-cube with wraparound links. (i) Calculate the total number of processors p, diameter D, node degree d, and bisection width B_w. (ii) Calculate the total number of physical links |C| and verify your result using the Handshaking Lemma (sum of degrees / 2).
solution: Diameter: D = d * floor(k / 2) = 3 * floor(4 / 2) = 3 * 2 = 6 hops.
Node degree: d_node = 2 * d = 2 * 3 = 6 (regular graph across all 64 nodes).
Verification via Handshaking Lemma: Total links = (1/2) * sum_{v} deg(v) = (64 * 6) / 2 = 384 / 2 = 192 links (Matches exactly!).

markingRubric.criterion: Correct calculation of p, D, degree, and B_w with formulas
Total links calculation and Handshaking Lemma verification

questions.question: In a 4-dimensional hypercube, a message must be routed from node S = 0101_2 to node D = 1110_2 using dimension-order (E-cube) routing. (i) Calculate the direction vector R = S XOR D and state the Hamming distance. (ii) List the complete sequence of intermediate nodes, dimensions traversed, and bits flipped. (iii) Explain why E-cube routing is guaranteed to be deadlock-free.
solution: (i) Direction vector: R = S XOR D = 0101_2 XOR 1110_2 = 1011_2. Hamming distance H(S, D) = 3 hops (bits 0, 1, and 3 differ; bit 2 is 1 in both).
(ii) Hop-by-hop traversal (resolving differing dimensions in increasing order 0, 1, 3):

(iii) Deadlock-freedom: Channels are acquired strictly in monotonic order of dimension (0 -> 1 -> 3). Because a channel in dimension i never waits for a channel in dimension j < i, the channel dependency graph is a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), which by Dally and Seitz's theorem guarantees absolute freedom from deadlock.

markingRubric.criterion: Correct XOR vector and Hamming distance
Accurate hop-by-hop path sequence and bit flips
Rigorous proof of deadlock freedom (DAG / monotonic dimension ordering)

questions.question: (i) Define Dilation, Congestion, and Expansion in graph embedding. (ii) Show how a 4x4 wraparound mesh can be embedded into a 4-D hypercube using 2-bit Reflected Gray Codes such that Dilation = 1, Congestion = 1, and Expansion = 1.
solution: - Dilation: Maximum length of a path in host graph G' corresponding to any single edge in guest graph G.
- Congestion: Maximum number of guest edges that share any single physical link in host graph G'.
- Expansion: Ratio of host nodes to guest nodes: |V'| / |V|.
- 2-bit Gray code sequence: G(0)=00, G(1)=01, G(2)=11, G(3)=10.
- Mapping function: For mesh node (r, c) with 0 <= r, c < 4, host node = G(r, 2) || G(c, 2).
- Example: Node (1, 1) maps to G(1, 2) || G(1, 2) = 0101_2.
- Each neighbor differs in exactly 1 bit, corresponding to an immediate physical link in the hypercube.

markingRubric.criterion: Accurate definitions of Dilation, Congestion, Expansion
Concatenated Gray code mapping function and neighbor verification

sections.title: Section 2: Vector Processors (Part D)
sections.description: Pipelining speedup, VMIPS architecture, strip-mining, and memory interleaving.

questions.question: A 4-segment pipelined arithmetic execution unit evaluates the expression R_i = A_i * B_i + C_i for n = 100 independent tasks. The clock period of the pipeline is 5 ns. (i) Derive the formula for pipelined execution time T_p and unpipelined execution time T_n. (ii) Calculate total cycles, total execution time in nanoseconds, and speedup for n = 100. (iii) What is the theoretical speedup as n -> infinity?
solution: - First task requires k clock cycles to exit the pipeline. Remaining n - 1 tasks exit at 1 task per cycle.
(iii) Theoretical limit: lim_{n -> inf} (n * k) / (k + n - 1) = k = 4.00x.

markingRubric.criterion: Derivation of T_p and T_n formulas
Correct calculation of cycles, nanoseconds, and speedup (3.88x)
Correct asymptotic limit (k = 4x)

questions.question: (i) Explain the strip-mining algorithm in vector architectures. (ii) If an array of n = 180 elements is processed on a vector architecture with Maximum Vector Length MVL = 64, calculate the total number of strip passes and the exact VLEN value for each pass. (iii) Write the corresponding VMIPS vector loop structure.
solution: (i) Strip-mining: When vector length n exceeds the physical hardware capacity MVL of a vector register, the loop is split into chunks of size <= MVL. The first pass handles the remainder n % MVL, and all subsequent passes process exactly MVL elements.
SLL   R2, R1, 3     ; Offset = VLEN * 8 bytes

markingRubric.criterion: Strip-mining conceptual definition
Correct pass count (3) and VLEN values (52, 64, 64)
Valid VMIPS assembly control flow

questions.question: (i) Contrast Array Processors (SIMD in space) with Vector Processors (SIMD in time). (ii) Explain why vector processors use memory interleaving and state when bank conflicts occur.
solution: - Array Processors (SIMD in Space): Replicates N independent ALUs across chip area. All N ALUs execute the same instruction simultaneously during the same clock cycle.
- Vector Processors (SIMD in Time): Uses a single (or few) deeply pipelined ALUs. Elements stream through pipeline stages sequentially across successive clock cycles.
- Pipelined vector functional units require 1-2 words per clock cycle. Standard single-bank DRAM is too slow (t_cycle > 1).
- Memory interleaving divides memory into M independent banks. Address A maps to bank A % M.
- Bank conflicts occur if a strided access hits the same bank before its recovery time t_cycle has elapsed (whenever gcd(stride, M) > 1). Odd strides prevent conflicts.

markingRubric.criterion: Rigorous space vs time comparison
Explanation of interleaving and bank conflict condition gcd(s, M) > 1

sections.title: Section 3: Performance Tools and Analysis (Part E)
sections.description: Amdahl vs Gustafson, Karp-Flatt metric, profiling vs tracing, and bottleneck diagnosis.

questions.question: (i) Derive Amdahl's Law for strong scaling and Gustafson's Law for weak scaling. (ii) An algorithm has a serial fraction s = 0.08 (8%). Calculate the theoretical speedup on 32 processors under Amdahl's Law and under Gustafson's Law. Explain the physical reason for the discrepancy.
solution: - Amdahl's Law (Strong Scaling): Fixed problem size. Serial fraction s, parallel fraction 1 - s. T(N) = s + (1 - s)/N. S(N) = 1 / [s + (1 - s)/N].
- Gustafson's Law (Weak Scaling): Problem size scales with N. Parallel execution time normalized to 1. T_seq = s + (1 - s)N. S(N) = N - s(N - 1).

(iii) Physical reason: Amdahl assumes a fixed workload where parallel portions shrink to zero while the serial 8% remains constant. Gustafson assumes workload grows proportionally with processor count, so the parallel work expands while the serial fraction remains a small constant time overhead.

markingRubric.criterion: Mathematical derivation of both laws
Correct numerical speedups (Amdahl = 9.20x, Gustafson = 29.52x)
Physical explanation of fixed vs scaled workload

questions.question: A parallel benchmark yields the following speedups on a cluster: on p = 4, S = 3.6; on p = 8, S = 6.4; on p = 16, S = 9.8. (i) Calculate the Karp-Flatt metric e for p = 4, 8, and 16. (ii) Based on the trend of e, diagnose whether the performance limitation is caused by an inherent serial code bottleneck or parallel communication overhead.
solution: (ii) Diagnosis: Value e remains roughly constant around 3.6% - 4.2% up to 8 processors, indicating an inherent serial fraction of approximately 3.7%. At p = 16, e begins rising (from 0.0357 to 0.0422), signaling that parallel communication and synchronization overheads are starting to compound.

markingRubric.criterion: Calculation of e for p = 4, 8, 16
Accurate diagnostic interpretation of constant vs increasing e

questions.question: (i) Contrast Profiling and Tracing across data volume, temporal visibility, and overhead. (ii) In an MPI application, Rank 0 takes 50 ms to compute a boundary region while Ranks 1-3 take 20 ms. What wait-state does Scalasca detect at the subsequent MPI_Recv? How does a timeline trace prove causality where a flat profile fails?
solution: - Data Volume: Profiling file size is compact and constant (KB-MB); Tracing file size scales linearly with time and event frequency (GB-TB).
- Temporal Visibility: Profiling aggregates time across the whole run (discards timeline); Tracing preserves full chronologically ordered event streams.
- Overhead: Profiling overhead is low (1-5%); Tracing overhead is moderate-to-high (5-30%+).
- Scalasca detects a 'Late Sender' wait-state on Ranks 1-3.
- Ranks 1-3 post MPI_Recv at t = 20 ms and sit idle for 30 ms waiting for Rank 0 to finish computing and post MPI_Send at t = 50 ms.

- Causality proof: A flat profile merely reports 30 ms spent in MPI_Recv (which looks like a slow receive); a timeline trace displays the timestamps of both sender and receiver, proving that the delay was actually caused by Rank 0's delayed computation.

markingRubric.criterion: Profiling vs Tracing comparative matrix
Late Sender identification and timeline causality explanation
